accuracy.evidence: Checked the science at an early-years level: heat flows from hotter to cooler things, so cocoa left out cools towards room temperature and never freezes on a table; ice melts in warm sun and stays frozen in a freezer; adding cold water lowers a bath's temperature and hot water raises it; a hot pan can look exactly like a cold one. The Development Matters wording for 3 and 4 year olds is quoted, and Celsius is correctly placed in Key Stage 2.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the ideas reported for this age: touching to check whether something is hot, expecting hot things to look red or steamy, thinking a drink left out gets hotter or icy, believing darkness rather than warmth melts ice, and using warm and hot as one word. Each one has a lab moment and its own Challenge message.

lab_distinct.evidence: The flagwarm lab is about temperature itself: a three-way hot, warm, cold sort, a kitchen safety hunt, a cocoa cup whose thermometer falls with each wait and goes cold if you wait too long, an ice lolly dragged to the sun or the freezer, and a bath run with hot and cold taps until a grown-up's elbow check says warm. The shingle gate against every other flag lab passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child finds out by doing: drinking too early gives too hot, waiting too long gives cold, so warm is the point in between; the lolly only melts where it is warm; the bath starts cold then hot, so the child learns which tap moves it which way. The step message confirms each idea after the child has seen it happen.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions are locked before the task, each with a tempting wrong choice: whether a pan without steam is safe to touch, whether cocoa on the table gets hotter, and whether the lolly melts in the freezer. The completion line repeats the locked guess and says what the child just saw.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions with every wrong option tagged: a hot drink chosen as cold, touch it to check, cocoa getting hotter or freezing on a table, the freezer or the dark melting a lolly, hot water or bubbles to cool a bath, and fire or snow as warm. Each tag has its own short message that names the slip.

readability.evidence: The kid text scores about grade -0.8 on the repo's Flesch-Kincaid check with sentences such as Ice is cold and Hot can hurt you. Card labels are one or two words with an emoji. The adult notes score about grade 9.2 and use the Development Matters terms Understanding the World and changes they notice.

no_filler.evidence: Every kid paragraph gives a hot, warm or cold example or a safety rule, and every adult paragraph is curriculum placement, the cause-and-effect science, named mistakes or what the lab does. The familyTip is three concrete activities (elbow test, ice cubes in sun and fridge, naming hot things in the kitchen). The filler scan passed.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px screenshots in light and dark: card and kitchen labels were shortened to one word and enlarged after the first pass so nothing clips, the bath was narrowed so the thermometer labels no longer overlap it, the three sort boxes fit side by side, and every control is a large young-layout button under the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: Every drag or tap has a labelled button (Ice is cold, Is the pan hot, Wait a little, Drink the cocoa, Put the lolly in the sun, Add hot water, A grown-up checks the bath), the canvas aria-label follows each spoken message, and the Challenge uses a labelled answer group with a polite live status line. axe passed in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
